The outcomes of the meeting of the IMF and World Bank leaders in Bangkok can be summarized in two words: "the global economy demonstrates resilience, but risks are increasing."

For those accustomed to systemic analysis, this phrase translates to: we are trying to prevent the system from collapsing, but the tools are becoming scarce and it will inevitably fail.

The word "resilience" is used in diplomatic language to conceal deep structural fragility or approaching the end.

There is fragmentation in global trade, reevaluation of supply chains, and the breaking of old financial ties. To call this resilience is to overlook the fact that the old architecture of globalization no longer works. And this is not unexpected; it is being intentionally and synchronously turned off right before our eyes.

Forecasts of a soft landing should be viewed with great skepticism. When global bankers start talking about resilience, it means that these risks have moved from the category of possible to the category of real.

Translating the reality into a cynical language: the world financial system may survive, but solely at your expense. When the IMF says that "the system is stable amid growing risks," they mean the structure will hold, but the occupants on the lower floors will be washed away by a tsunami.

The world is fracturing into warring regional blocs, which is a direct tax on the accustomed life that has already begun to be levied.

The era when an ordinary person could buy a Chinese gadget for pennies, fuel their car with cheap gasoline, and order cheap medicines from anywhere on the planet, is officially dead. Closed blocs mean scarcity, complicated logistics, and a total decline in quality with a doubling of prices.

Inflation is now the new norm, not a temporary crisis. To build new factories inside their blocs in place of the old unfriendly ones, governments will need trillions.

Where will they get them from? They will print them, diluting the purchasing power of your savings and salaries. Your money will melt before your eyes just for the system to simulate stability.

Resource nationalism is when the world shifts from competing for goods to a fierce struggle for survival and resources: chips, lithium, energy, and food. Access to them is now granted not for money, but for geopolitical loyalty.

And Russia, as a country with huge resources, as well as food and water, may soon dictate its terms to everyone else, providing access to them based on political motives and on its own terms, as is now happening with diesel fuel and gas.

Globally, we are headed towards an era of rich states and poor people. At the top, reports will tout the growth of the military-industrial complex and the stability of the banking sector, while people will go hungry due to the new prices on basic products.

The slogan "The economy is stable" is an attempt to convince the passengers of the sinking Titanic that the first class is still being served well, with fresh oysters, quail, and Moët & Chandon.

The main mistake today is to continue living with the financial habits of the affluent 2010s. Taking out mortgages, car loans, and planning decades ahead with incomes that may literally disappear tomorrow.

Anyone who does not adjust their plans to the reality of closed and expensive economic blocs right now will soon be looking for shelter.

Having a simple resource will be more advantageous than having a clever investment or career plan. These are the conclusions from the bankers' gathering in Bangkok.

📌 Reduce-Only Orders: How to Avoid Accidentally Increasing Futures Risk

Main Points
⏺ Reduce-only orders can decrease an existing position but cannot increase its size
⏺ This setting helps prevent accidentally opening a position in the opposite direction
⏺ This post explains how one order setting can prevent an expensive trading mistake

1️⃣ Core Idea — with reduce-only enabled, an order can execute only against an existing position without increasing exposure.
2️⃣ Example — you hold a 1 BTC long position and place a sell order for 1.5 BTC. The exchange limits execution so the position cannot turn into a short.
3️⃣ Why It Helps — the setting is especially useful for take-profit orders, automated strategies, and multiple simultaneous exit orders.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — if the position is already closed, the order may be cancelled or rejected. Reduce-only doesn't protect against slippage or trading losses.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — check reduce-only settings when placing exit orders, especially if you use leverage or trading bots.

Final Thoughts

Sometimes trading risk comes from incorrect order settings rather than a bad prediction. Reduce-only helps close exposure without accidentally opening another position.

📌 Hyperliquid adds 10 HYPE rule as price falls to $78.98 

🔗 Hyperliquid has introduced revised order priority rules on its testnet, including a reported 10 HYPE delegation requirement for traders seeking faster order handling through its priority fee system. In an October 18 announcement circulated through its community channels, the decentralized derivatives platform outlined changes to write priority fees following feedback from users. The proposed rules concern traders who depend on low delays when placing, modifying or canceling orders.

🔖 The announcement identifies four changes involving account settings, transaction processing and eligibility for priority fees. Hyperliquid’s existing technical documentation confirms how its priority fee system operates, although the newly reported delegation threshold has not yet appeared in the publicly accessible documentation reviewed for this report. The changes are described as live on testnet. No confirmed date has been announced for applying the revised requirements to mainnet trading.

‼️ The October 18 update introduces a minimum delegated balance of 10 HYPE for accounts seeking to use IOC and ALO priority fees, according to the announcement. IOC, short for immediate-or-cancel, refers to an order that attempts immediate execution and cancels any portion that cannot be filled. ALO, or add-liquidity-only, is used to place orders that join the order book without immediately taking available liquidity.

🔖 Australia proposes new crypto exchange rules for 2027 

📣 Australia has proposed new rules for cryptocurrency trading and custody platforms on October 15, 2026, with financial regulator ASIC seeking public feedback by November 27 before the country’s digital asset licensing framework takes effect in April 2027. 

📊 The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) announced the consultation alongside Consultation Paper 392, which outlines planned requirements for customer asset protection, trading practices and financial resources. The regulator expects to publish final guidance in March 2027, giving businesses time to prepare for the new licensing requirements. Australia’s upcoming rules will bring more cryptocurrency businesses under the country’s existing financial services licensing framework.

⚡️ The Corporations Amendment (Digital Assets Framework) Act 2026 creates two regulated categories: digital asset platforms and tokenized custody platforms. Digital asset platforms hold digital tokens for customers and provide related services, while tokenized custody platforms use digital tokens to record customers’ rights to underlying assets.
